extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and advanced students interested in scientific method and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding and evaluating the assumptions, scope, and epistemic status of scientific inference, experiment, classification, and explanation; i.e., how and when scientific method yields reliable knowledge and where it faces unavoidable limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions of inductive inference
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductive inference involves the assumption that our knowledge of what exists is complete, and that the conditions of things remain unaltered between the time of our experience and the time to which our inferences refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the ballot-box simile: when predicting the next draw we assume (1) previous drawings have been sufficiently numerous to give knowledge of the box contents and (2) no interference occurs between previous and next drawings. If these assumptions fail, inductive inference is undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required for applicability of probability theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The results yielded by the theory of probability are valid only when the sampling conditions are appropriate (sufficient past data and absence of interference); otherwise the theory ceases to be applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No finite number of casual drawings can give sure knowledge; probability-theoretic conclusions are relative to information. If arbitrary unknown interference is possible, there ceases to be any connection between premises and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional and relative status of scientific conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions of scientific inference are always hypothetical and provisional; the best-calculated results are never absolute probabilities but are relative to the extent of our information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We cannot be sure how far our experience gives adequate information of the universe as a whole, hence scientific conclusions should be treated as the best current interpretation, not as final certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of scientific method regarding metaphysical possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific method cannot disprove certain metaphysical possibilities (e.g., 'Divine interference' in nature); absence of a scientific refutation does not eliminate such possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such interference might take forms that evade empirical detection (disclosure of unknown agents, pre-arranged changes of law, creation or annihilation of portions of nature). Science's inability to exclude these does not imply endorsement, only epistemic limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical laws are high-probability hypotheses, not geometric certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles like the indestructibility of matter and conservation of energy are very probable scientific hypotheses but are not certain in the same absolute sense as a geometrical proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a gross misconception to treat such empirical laws as absolutely certain; they accord with past experiments but remain hypotheses whose certainty is limited by the extent of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method must begin and end with laws of thought but cannot prevent paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific reasoning is grounded in the basic laws of thought (identity, difference, duality), yet this grounding does not guarantee avoidance of apparently inexplicable or contradictory results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: difficulties arising from continuous quantity (infinite subdivisions), mathematical theorems that clash with common spatial intuition, and functions with surprising limiting behaviour. Recognize and tolerate such paradoxical-seeming outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to record and investigate all phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: One unquestionable rule of scientific method is that whatever phenomenon exists must not be ignored; existing phenomena demand explanation and scientific investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We must not dismiss phenomena because they conflict with current theory or are not immediately measurable; recording and investigating phenomena (including human instincts and consciousness) is a legitimate scientific task that competes for recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of explanatory theories (e.g., evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories (such as Darwinian evolution) may show general principles and numerous adaptations but do not necessarily provide a 'complete explanation of any single living form' or account for why particular historical contingencies resulted in the exact forms we observe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theories to explicate general mechanisms and patterns, but acknowledge that they often raise further indeterminate problems about unique historical outcomes and contingent events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental integrity: maintain comparable conditions and prevent interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity of experimental inference requires that conditions remain comparable between observations and that no unknown or arbitrary interference occurs during the interval between observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unknown interference (including changes in law or tampering) can render experimental and probabilistic reasoning inapplicable. Design experiments to control or rule out such interferences (e.g., blind tests, controls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic modesty and openness to non-measurable aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: True scientific attitude combines rigorous empiricism with modesty: do not deny the existence of things merely because they cannot currently be weighed or measured; accept that reality may contain wonders and subtleties beyond present perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain openness to intellectual existences not localized in space/time and avoid dogmatic positivism that dismisses non-empirical dimensions of possible existence.
